**before this change as well as after**, so native rejects re-constraining an already-bound
variable inside a subquery and TS accepts it. Together with item 154's `path` finding (reserved

## 156. A keyed-join count is a sum of products, not an enumeration — 44x, and neither engine had it

Item 154's gap table left the keyed join at 18.5x. Diagnosing it first killed the obvious theory
and then found a better target.

### The join itself is not a missing path

The second pattern is correlated (`q` already bound), so the question was whether TS reverse-walks
from `q` or rescans the `b:P` bucket per outer row. Those are distinguished by varying the BUCKET
independently of the edges — adding `P` vertices with no edges at all, which a reverse walk never
looks at:

| bucket | keyed join (ts) | one pattern (ts) | scan (ts) |
| -----: | --------------: | ---------------: | --------: |
|  2,000 |           5.357 |            1.284 |     0.519 |
|  6,000 |           4.254 |            2.255 |     1.686 |
| 18,000 |           8.167 |            5.038 |     5.100 |

A rescan would be 2,000 x 18,000 and take seconds. The join's own cost (the difference from the
one-pattern row) stays ~1.5-2µs per outer row across the sweep, so it is **per-row machinery, the
same constant factor as item 155**, not a missing path.

### The count IS one

`keyed join count` measured **74-92x** behind native — and it has a closed form. The shared
variable is `q`, so

```
count = SUM over q of  c1(q) x c2(q)
```

where `cN(q)` counts side N's edges landing on `q` whose far end satisfies that side's own
constraints. Unconstrained that is SUM of indeg(q)², and the pairs include the diagonal (`a` and
`b` are distinct variables with no inequality between them), which the square gets right for
free. This is exactly the branch `productCountOf` refuses by design — "a shared variable is a
JOIN, not a product" — and a join is a SUM of products, one per shared value.

**My first reading of native was wrong.** I inferred native had a shortcut from its 0.044ms. It
does not: 0.030ms at 2,870 pairs and 0.945ms at 73,810 is linear in PAIRS. Native enumerates
too, just ~50x faster per pair. So this is not catching up — **neither engine had the closed
form**, and TS now beats native on it.

**A ring fixture cannot test any of this**, which the first probe was. With every in-degree 1,
`SUM d²`, `SUM d` and the edge count all coincide, so a wrong formula agrees with a right one.
The fixtures here use hub-and-spoke with in-degrees 1..n, and the expected value is computed
independently in JS so both engines are checked against arithmetic rather than each other.

### Measured

| fixture                   | before | after |     ratio |        vs native |
| ------------------------- | -----: | ----: | --------: | ---------------: |
| 20 hubs, in-degrees 1..20 |  1.613 | 0.234 |  **6.9x** |     53.3x → 8.3x |
| 60 hubs, in-degrees 1..60 | 30.245 | 0.683 | **44.0x** | 32.0x → **0.9x** |

The win GROWS with degree (6.9x → 44x) because the work goes from O(pairs) to O(V + E) — 73,810
pairs against 1,830 edges on the larger fixture. At 60 hubs TS is now slightly faster than
native. Answers verified against the independently computed `SUM indeg²` at both sizes.

### Teeth: 29 tests, 7 of 8 mutants caught

**Every test checks the shortcut against the ENUMERATION of the same pattern**, which is
`productCountOf`'s own rule: the oracle is what the engine already returns, not an argument from
what the shape ought to mean. A count asserted against a hand-computed number would only prove
the author and the code agree.

| mutant                                  | result                    |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| SUM instead of PRODUCT per shared value | caught — 13 failures      |
| direction inverted                      | caught — 12 failures      |
| far-end INLINE check dropped            | caught — 3 failures       |
| far-end LABEL check dropped             | caught                    |
| shared-vertex LABEL check dropped       | caught                    |
| shared-vertex INLINE check dropped      | caught                    |
| shared variable at the START allowed    | caught, after a test      |
| two shared variables allowed            | **survives** — equivalent |

Each mutation was verified to have landed (`grep -cF` of the target before running), after item
155 found four silently applied to the wrong function.

**The two survivors were both masked by a neighbouring guard, and only one was a test gap.**
Dropping "the start must not be the shared variable" changed nothing until a pattern existed
whose shared variable is BOTH ends — `(q)-[:E]->(q)`, a self-loop requirement — because every
other shared-at-start shape is already refused by "the endpoint must be the shared variable".
Two tests added for it. The remaining survivor is genuinely equivalent: with two or more shared
variables, `patternVarsOf` returns the start first, so `shared[0]` is always a pattern's START
and the endpoint guard declines before the count check matters.

29 patterns compared FOUR ways — TS count, TS enumeration, native count, native enumeration —
covering both spellings, both directions, mixed directions, different types per side, far-end
labels/props/predicates, shared-vertex constraints from either pattern, parallel edges, a
self-loop, `$param` bounds, and every declining shape. All agree.

### A pre-existing NATIVE wrong answer, found and recorded

One pattern diverges, and it is not the shortcut's:

```
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P WHERE b.k > 1)-[:E]->(q) RETURN count(*)
   ts 3   (= its own enumeration, 3 rows)
  nat 1   (= its own enumeration, 1 row)
```

Each engine is SELF-CONSISTENT, so they disagree about what the query means rather than about
counting — and it is **identical before this change**. Working it by hand on the fixture, side 2
admits exactly one source and the shared vertex it reaches has in-degree 3, so 3 x 1 = 3: TS is
right. Native appears to apply pattern 2's inline predicate to pattern 1's variable as well, a
predicate leaking across patterns. A node predicate alone agrees (2 = 2), so it is specific to
the multi-pattern case.

That is the **third** cross-engine divergence recorded in three ticks, and the first that is a
WRONG ANSWER rather than a parse difference (item 154: `path` reserved in TS only; item 155: a
subquery re-constraining a bound variable). All three are in native and none is caused by this
work. They are now the most valuable open items in this audit — byte-identity is the hard
invariant, and a wrong count outranks any remaining perf gap.

Gates separately: 29 new tests (821 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0 — it caught a real shadowed parameter in this change, and its custom
`lenke(no-raw-interpolation)` rule flagged the scratch probes — `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0,
all seven byte-identity fuzzers green on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 157. A continuing MATCH's inline WHERE clobbered the parser's scope — a wrong count, a bogus error, and a panic

Item 156 found native returning 1 where TS returned 3, each engine agreeing with its OWN
enumeration. This is the cause, and it turned out to be a cluster rather than one bug. **No perf
work this item** — byte-identity is the hard invariant and a wrong answer outranks the remaining
perf gaps.

### Diagnosis

Dumping native's plan and running the shape's neighbours separated what broke from what did not:

```
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P WHERE b.k > 1)-[:E]->(q) RETURN count(*)   nat 1, ts 3
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P WHERE b.k > 1)-[:E]->(q) RETURN a.k, b.k   nat PARSE ERROR
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P), (b:P WHERE b.k > 1)-[:E]->(q) RETURN a.k, b.k        nat 3 rows ✓
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P {k: 2})-[:E]->(q) RETURN a.k, b.k          nat 3 rows ✓
MATCH (a:P WHERE a.k > 1)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P)-[:E]->(q) RETURN a.k, b.k   nat 3 rows ✓
```

The enumerating spelling raised **`unknown variable a`** — for a query whose `a` is plainly
bound. Only a continuing `MATCH` whose pattern carries an inline `WHERE` was affected; the comma
spelling, the inline-props spelling and a predicate on the FIRST pattern were all correct, which
is why this survived.

`match_continue` and `extend_chain` had five sites doing

```rust
self.scope = scope.clone();                 // no restore
plan = plan.filter(self.parse_captured_where(r)?);
```

The predicate does need the sub-pattern's slot space — but leaving it there has three
consequences:

1. **A silently wrong join key.** `match_continue` computes it three lines later by looking each
   sub variable up in `self.scope`, which by then IS the sub scope — so every sub slot matched
   ITSELF and the key came out `[(0, 0), (1, 1)]`, joining `a` to `b` as well as `q` to `q`.
   The count of 1 was the number of pairs where `a` happened to equal `b`.
2. **Outer names gone**, hence `unknown variable a` at RETURN.
3. **A PANIC.** `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P)-[e:E WHERE e.w >= 0]->(z:P)` panicked in
   `batch.rs` — `index out of bounds: the len is 2 but the index is 2` — surfacing to the caller
   as a misleading `E_INVALID_VALUE`. A predicate compiled against one slot space, evaluated
   against another.

**The correct idiom was already in the same function**, forty lines away (save, set, parse,
restore, at the per-hop `rel.where_range`). These five were oversights against the file's own
pattern, which is the detail worth remembering: the fix is not a new technique, it is applying
the existing one consistently.

### The fix, and what it moved

`std::mem::replace` to set the sub scope, parse, then put the caller's scope back, at all five
sites. Measured on a 24-shape differential probe against TS:

|        |   diverging |
| ------ | ----------: |
| before | **14 / 24** |
| after  |  **2 / 24** |

and the panic is gone. The two that remain are both LOUD refusals in native, not wrong answers:

- `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P WHERE b.k = a.k)-[:E]->(q)` — an inline `WHERE`
  referencing an OUTER variable. TS correlates it (4); native raises `E_SYNTAX`. A missing
  feature: the predicate spans both slot spaces, so it has to be lowered as a post-join filter.
- `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH ((b:P)-[:E]->(z:P) WHERE z.k = 9)` — a parenthesized pattern
  with its own `WHERE` in a continuing MATCH. Native raises `E_SYNTAX`; unsupported syntax.

Both are recorded as open; neither can return a wrong answer.

### Teeth: 11 tests, 3 of 5 mutants caught — and the other two are honest

Each test pins an answer, and **the oracle is the equivalent spelling that never reached the
clobbered line** — the comma form or the trailing-`WHERE` form. Those were always right, which
is exactly what made the bug invisible.

| mutant (restore removed at)         | result              |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `match_continue`'s fresh-start site | caught — 6 failures |
| the plain hop's landing-node site   | caught — 1 failure  |
| the inline-edge-`WHERE` site        | caught — 2 failures |
| the quantified landing-node site    | **survives**        |
| the quantified group-variable site  | **survives**        |

The two quantified sites survive even after adding tests aimed squarely at them (a `{1,2}`
continuing pattern with a landing predicate, and one with a per-hop edge predicate — both now in
the suite, both agreeing with their comma-spelling oracle). I could not construct a shape where
those restores are observable. **The code says so**: they are kept for CONSISTENCY with the three
that are load-bearing, not because a test proves they matter — and an inconsistent pattern across
five neighbouring sites is precisely what produced this bug.

**A test expectation of mine was wrong, and the test said so.** The node-only shape
`MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P WHERE b.k > 1)` I wrote as 3 pattern rows x 1 qualifying
node = 3. It is 6: the SHARED vertex carries `k = 9`, which also passes `k > 1`. The comment now
records the slip and the assertion leans on the comma-spelling oracle rather than on arithmetic
in a comment.

## 158. A continuing MATCH's inline WHERE may now read an outer variable

Item 157 left two divergences open, both LOUD refusals in native. This closes the first:

```
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH (b:P WHERE b.k = a.k)-[:E]->(q) RETURN count(*)
   ts 3
  nat RAISE unknown variable `a`
```

TS correlates the predicate; native refused it. This is a missing FEATURE rather than a wrong
answer — which is why it came after item 157 and not before.

### Why it could not simply be parsed

A continuing `MATCH`'s pattern is parsed in its OWN slot space (0-based) and joined with the
working table afterwards, so a predicate reading both `b` (slot 0 of the new pattern) and `a`
(a slot of the working table) refers to two different coordinate systems. Resolving it against
either one alone fails — which is exactly what the `unknown variable` was.

**The deferral needs no remapping at all**, which is what makes this small. By the time the join
is built, `match_continue` has already merged the new pattern's variables into `self.scope` at
`width + r`, alongside the outer names at their own slots. Parsing the captured span at that
point — rather than before the join — resolves both halves correctly, and the predicate becomes
a filter on the joined plan.

**The split is kept deliberately.** A predicate reading only its own variables still filters the
pattern's SEED, where it prunes before the expansion; only a correlated one is deferred. Mutation
confirms the split is load-bearing in one direction and free in the other (below).

### Deciding which route, before parsing

The span cannot be parsed until the route is chosen, so the decision scans its TOKENS for an
identifier that is in the outer scope and not among the pattern's own bindings.

A property name is also an `Ident`, so `(b WHERE b.a = 1)` with an outer variable called `a`
reports an outer read and takes the after-join route. **The error is one-sided by construction**:
a false positive is slower and still correct, and a false negative — which would be the bug —
cannot happen, because every genuine outer name is in `self.scope`. A test pins the
false-positive case's answer.

### Verified

A 23-shape differential probe against TS: **all agree**, covering the new correlated forms
(`=`, `>`, `<>`, mixed with an own-variable conjunct, with a trailing clause `WHERE`, on an
uncorrelated pattern, reading the outer pattern's FAR end, on a node-only pattern, after a
`WITH`) and every shape item 157 established, so the probe is the cluster's regression check.

### Teeth: 10 tests, 2 of 4 mutants caught, both survivors one-sided

**The oracle is the trailing-`WHERE` spelling** — `MATCH … MATCH (b:P)-[:E]->(q) WHERE b.k = a.k`
— which expresses the same question and was always supported. Every test asserts the two agree,
so none rests on arithmetic in a comment.

| mutant                                      | result              |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| never defer (always filter the seed)        | caught — 8 failures |
| deferred predicate parsed but never applied | caught — 8 failures |
| ALWAYS defer (never filter the seed)        | **survives**        |
| detector ignores the own-variables set      | **survives**        |

Both survivors widen the deferral, which is **correct but slower** — the same one-sidedness the
token scan relies on. They are not test gaps: deferring a predicate that could have filtered the
seed gives the same rows, and no test can assert "this was applied earlier" without a timing
threshold. The code says which direction is safe and why.

(The "never applied" mutant was a NO-OP on its first run — the `perl` pattern did not match. Caught
by the `applied=` check that items 155-156 added to the loop, then re-applied by line number,
where it failed immediately. That check has now earned itself twice.)

Gates separately: 10 new tests (952 engine tests pass), engine-core's 34 pass, clippy
`-D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `rewrite_fuzz` and `fastpath_fuzz` green, the
TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green on random seeds.
Mutation ran under `timeout 900` plus `MemoryMax=16G MemorySwapMax=0`.

### What remains in this cluster

One divergence, still open and still a loud refusal: a parenthesized pattern with its own
`WHERE` in a continuing MATCH — `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(q:P) MATCH ((b:P)-[:E]->(z:P) WHERE z.k = 9)`
— which native rejects as `E_SYNTAX`. Unsupported syntax rather than a scope problem, so it is a
separate piece of work.

## 159. The fused hop projection carries a far-end filter — 4.3-7.4x, at a measured 1.24x on the unfiltered hop

Back to perf after items 157-158. Re-deriving the gap table (items 154-158 changed the GQL
engine four times, so the old one was driving target selection on stale numbers) put one row far
ahead of the rest:

```
shape                     ts        native     gap
Expand + FAR filter       29.166    0.108      268.9x
Expand + far INLINE       15.553    0.106      147.4x
Expand out (no filter)     6.343    2.659        2.4x
```

**A filter that cuts 20,000 rows to 207 made the query 4.6x SLOWER than the unfiltered hop.** As
in item 154, that is a declined fast path, not the cost of filtering — and sweeping selectivity
confirmed it: TS cost 19.0 / 24.3 / 26.5ms for 0 / 207 / 20,000 surviving rows, i.e. flat in the
answer and proportional to the bucket. `detectHopProjection` declined on `m.where !== undefined`,
with the comment "a clause `WHERE` would have to be evaluated per row, which is the general
path's job."

### Carried, both spellings

The compiled clause `WHERE` the general path uses is applied inside the fused walk, once per row
after both endpoints are bound — the general path's own point, so the evaluation count and the
elements evaluated are unchanged (the items-139/142 rule).

**And the far node's own inline constraint too, which was not optional.** Making only the clause
form fast would have left the two spellings of one question 5x apart (2.5ms against 13ms) — the
gap this repo is named after, newly created by the fix. `satisfies` is the general path's node
check and needs no allocation, since the single mutated binding already holds the far end.
CLOSED constraints only, the rule `inlineOf` applies: `(v {k: u.k})` is correlated and declines.

**A measured boundary, not a conservative one.** A `WHERE` reading only the START is refused and
left to item 154's seed pre-filter, which evaluates it once per start VERTEX and skips the
expansion; carrying it here evaluated it per EDGE and cost 4.047 → 5.228ms. The first version of
this change had no such guard and regressed that shape.

### The layout cost, and four arrangements to minimise it

The hot UNFILTERED hop notices the change even though nothing about it is functionally
different. All four arrangements were measured interleaved, min-of-three:

| arrangement                                      | unfiltered hop |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------: |
| filter checks folded into the one existing loop  |    1.6x slower |
| two MODULE-SCOPE walks taking a spec object      |   1.29x slower |
| two closures built inside the detect function    |   1.25x slower |
| **unfiltered inline, filtered behind a factory** |      **1.24x** |

The middle one is the instructive failure. `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` says to keep a walk
at module scope, and it is right about closure SIZE — but a SHARED module-scope walk is called
with every compile's shapes, so its call sites go polymorphic, and destructuring the spec into
locals did not recover it. Two effects pull opposite ways; a factory gives each compile its own
closure AND keeps the detect function small, which is what both want.

### Measured, interleaved, min-of-three each side, isolated harness

| shape                    | before | after |    ratio |
| ------------------------ | -----: | ----: | -------: |
| far INLINE filter        | 13.586 | 1.829 | **7.4x** |
| far CLAUSE filter        | 15.530 | 3.640 | **4.3x** |
| unfiltered hop (CONTROL) |  2.587 | 3.206 |    1.24x |

The control's ranges OVERLAP (before 2.59-3.47, after 3.21-4.15), so the honest statement is
flat-to-25% on the unfiltered hop for 4.3-7.4x on the filtered ones. That trade is the same shape
as item 149's (≈20% on the unseekable path for 10-43x on the seekable one) and is accepted on the
same grounds; four arrangements say 1.24x is the floor without a larger restructure.

This needed its own harness: the multi-shape probe put the untouched inline spelling at 1.15-1.27x
WORSE, which the isolated runs retracted (it is 7.4x faster). **Seventh retraction of a
multi-probe reading in this audit** (items 141, 143, 145, 151, 153, 157).

### Teeth: 18 tests, 4 of 5 mutants caught

**The oracle is independent**: every filtered result is compared against the UNFILTERED rows
filtered in JS, which does not rely on either engine's filtering being right. The two-ended case
compares against a projection reading the start, which declines to the general path.

| mutant                                    | result                        |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| carried clause `WHERE` never applied      | caught — 8 here, 11 in gql    |
| far-end inline predicate never applied    | caught — 5 here, 6 in gql     |
| closedness check on inline props dropped  | caught                        |
| start never bound for a two-ended `WHERE` | caught                        |
| the far-read requirement dropped          | **survives** — answer-neutral |

The survivor is the perf boundary above: carrying a start-only `WHERE` returns the same rows, so
no test can catch it and a timing threshold would be flaky. Its numbers are in the code.

One of my test expectations was wrong again and the test said so: the two-ended case I wrote as
`oracle(...).slice(0, 1)`, which is simply the wrong count — two edges leave the qualifying start
vertex. It now uses a real oracle instead of a slice.

`bun run lint` caught two real things in this change — a complexity of 46 against a limit of 35,
and an array-destructuring nit. The complexity was fixed the way this file already handles that
gate (item 143 split `distinctShape` out for the same reason): two helpers, `carriedWhere` and
`closedFarPred`.

### Recorded, not acted on

- `MATCH (u)-[:E]->(v) WHERE v.score = 5 RETURN u.name` — projecting the START under a far
  filter — still takes the general path at ~21ms, because the projection guard admits only the
  far variable. Binding the start for the projection is cheap and the next thing to try here.
- Native refuses `WHERE` inside `OPTIONAL MATCH` (`E_NOT_IMPLEMENTED`) where TS answers it. A
  fourth loud-refusal divergence, found while building the sweep.
- The full TS suite failed ONCE during this item and did not reproduce in two further full runs
  or three isolated runs of the implicated package; nx flagged `@lenke/native:test` and
  `@lenke/sync:test` as flaky in that run, the latter being the already-recorded timing flake.
  The output was not captured, so this is logged rather than diagnosed.

Gates separately: 18 new tests (839 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green on random seeds. No
Rust changed, so `bench_all` does not apply; the cross-engine `bun run bench` is the screen.

The screen moved three cells and all three are FASTER (`encode pg-text` 0.81x, `encode pg-json`

## 160. The fused hop projection may project the START — 4.1-6.6x, including an ordinary unfiltered hop

Item 159 left this, and its guard's own comment had already named the reason: projected items
could read only the FAR variable, because "an item reading the start would need it bound too
(cheap)". The machinery arrived in item 159 — the filtered walk binds the start when a carried
predicate reads it — so only the guard was left.

### What it cost

Projecting the start declined in EVERY shape, including ones with no filter at all:

| shape                        |     ts | ts projecting the far end |
| ---------------------------- | -----: | ------------------------: |
| far filter, project START    | 24.296 |                     5.120 |
| far filter, project BOTH     | 21.226 |                     5.120 |
| **no filter, project START** | 20.011 |                 **5.721** |
| no filter, project BOTH      | 23.477 |                     5.721 |
| far inline, project START    | 16.249 |                         — |

The third row is the one that matters most: `MATCH (u:L)-[:E]->(v) RETURN u.name` is as ordinary
a query as this engine gets, and it cost 3.5x the identical query projecting `v.name` instead —
two shapes with no semantic difference between them.

### The change, and why the routing matters

The item guard now admits EITHER endpoint; a name that is neither still declines, which is the
safety that was actually load-bearing (`freePredicateVars` cannot tell a name it does not
recognize from one it does, and the REL variable is refused earlier).

**The plain walk is left untouched.** Item 159 measured that adding even a branch to its inner
loop costs the hot far-only shape 1.6x, so a start-reading projection is routed to the FILTERED
walk instead — which already binds the start per vertex. It pays two always-false predicate
checks per edge, which is nothing against the 3.5x it gains, and the far-only path keeps the
exact body item 159 settled on.

### Measured, interleaved, min-of-three

| shape                      | before | after |    ratio |
| -------------------------- | -----: | ----: | -------: |
| no filter, project START   | 17.803 | 2.691 | **6.6x** |
| no filter, project BOTH    | 22.810 | 4.078 | **5.6x** |
| far filter, project BOTH   | 19.254 | 4.130 | **4.7x** |
| far filter, project START  | 23.473 | 5.719 | **4.1x** |
| far inline, project START  | 17.626 | 4.343 | **4.1x** |
| plain far-only (CONTROL)   |  2.405 | 2.736 |     flat |
| near filter, project START |  3.502 | 4.235 |     flat |

TS now sits at parity or better than native on the unfiltered projections (0.9x and 0.8x), where
it was 7.9x and 6.6x behind.

The control needed its own isolated harness, again: the multi-shape probe put the untouched
far-only walk at 3.699 before against 5.391/6.026 after, which looked like a real 1.5x. Isolated,
min-of-three a side, it is 2.405-3.237 before against 2.736-2.955 after — **overlapping ranges,
flat**. That is the EIGHTH retraction of a multi-probe reading in this audit, and the second time
this exact control has been over-read.

| mutant                                         | result                      |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `itemsReadStart` never set                     | caught — 10 here, 18 in gql |
| `needsStart` ignores the projection            | caught — 10 here, 18 in gql |
| routing ignores `needsStart` (plain walk used) | caught — 5 here, 8 in gql   |
| the start never bound in the filtered walk     | caught — 10 here, 19 in gql |

**Projecting the start is where a hop's DUPLICATES live** — one row per EDGE, so a vertex with
three out-edges appears three times. The fixture gives `a` three out-edges and `b` one for that

**Three test expectations of mine were wrong, and the tests said so.** Two wrote the expected

## 161. A property read was a hash lookup — 8.8x on the read, and three "structural" rows were not

The hop-projection family was exhausted, so this went to an axis the loop had not touched: the
TS **Gremlin** engine, a separate implementation with its own executor. Items 130-134 had
measured it and closed three rows as STRUCTURAL, with the note **"do not build a tally for any
of them"**:

```
V().has('age', gt).count()     47 / 0.38    73% property-bag reads
groupCount().by('age')         48 / 2.8     80.3% property-bag reads
V().out(T).values('age')      593 / 32      projecting, inherently per-row
```

That conclusion was right about tallies and wrong about the ceiling. "73% property-bag reads" is
a description, not an explanation — so this priced the read itself.

### The read

`Vertex.properties` was `graph.elementProperties.get(this.#id)` — a **STRING-KEYED `Map.get`**
into a map with one entry per element. Four ways of reading one property from each of 200,000
vertices, with 1,000,000 edges resident (item 134's lesson: data the query never touches still
decides the cache regime, so omitting the edges would be a different measurement):

|                                                           |        ms |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| `v.properties.age` — what both engines did                |     16.17 |
| the same with the bag hoisted (one read either way)       |     15.47 |
| **a dense array index — the ceiling**                     |  **0.23** |
| **the id-keyed `Map.get` ALONE, discarding the property** | **11.76** |

81ns per property read, of which **73% is the hash lookup** — which is exactly the share the
profiler attributed to "property-bag reads". The hoisted row shows the getter call itself is
free, so there was nothing to hoist; the cost was always the lookup.

### A BOX, not a cached bag

`Graph.elementProperties` now holds `{ bag }` rather than the bag, and each element caches its
box on first read. A read is a field load plus one property access; no lookup.

**It has to be a box**, and the reason is in `Graph`'s own test suite: `new Vertex({ id, graph })`
outside `addVertex` is a real construction path, so TWO ATTACHED instances can share one id.
Caching the bag would let the first go stale the moment the second wrote — silently. Both take
the same box from the map, and a write replaces `box.bag`, so there is still exactly one source
of truth per id. The bag itself stays frozen, so a stray `v.properties.x = …` still throws.

The invalidation has exactly three cases, and each is a test because each would be a silent
wrong read rather than an error:

- **two instances sharing an id** — a write through either must be visible through both;
- **an element moved to another graph** (`set graph`) — the box belongs to the OLD graph's map,
  so the cache is dropped;
- **an evicted element** — reads `{}` as it did before, which the `!this.#graph` guard preserves.

The whole change is three files and a type: the getter and `#commitProperties` in `Vertex` and
`Edge` (which that method's own comment already called "the single funnel for every property
write"), plus the map's value type. `elementProperties` had only 8 references repo-wide.

### Measured

**The read: 16.17ms → 1.83ms, 8.8x** (the 0.23ms ceiling is a dense array with no element
indirection at all, so 1.83 is the realistic floor for a cached reference).

Gremlin, interleaved, min-of-five — and **native's column is identical throughout**, which is
the ideal control since a TS core change cannot touch it:

| traversal                    |             before |              after |    ratio | gap vs native |
| ---------------------------- | -----------------: | -----------------: | -------: | ------------: |
| `V().has(age,gt).count()`    |               40.8 |                6.0 | **6.8x** |  125x → 17.5x |
| `V().groupCount(age)`        |               38.8 |                7.4 | **5.2x** |  13.7x → 2.6x |
| `V().out().has().count()`    |              251.1 |              128.1 | **2.0x** |  166x → 85.5x |
| `V().out().values(age)`      |              580.5 |              548.7 |    1.06x |             — |
| `V().out().dedupe().count()` |                6.5 |                6.9 |     flat |             — |
| the O(1) shortcut rows       |                0.0 |                0.0 |     flat |             — |
| native (CONTROL, every row)  | 0.33 / 2.83 / 1.51 | 0.34 / 2.89 / 1.50 |     flat |             — |

Two of the three "structural" rows moved 6.8x and 5.2x — **not by building a tally, but by
fixing the read underneath them**. The third (`values(age)`) barely moves, which is consistent
with its diagnosis: it is projection-bound, not read-bound.

**And it is not a Gremlin fix.** The cross-engine screen moved SEVEN cells and every one is
faster, because this read is under the GQL engine and the codecs too:

| row                             | before |  after |          |
| ------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -------: |
| `query: group + aggregate`      |  19.30 |   9.10 | **2.1x** |
| `traverse 1-hop + start filter` | 101.60 |  61.80 | **1.6x** |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`       | 129.80 |  86.80 | **1.5x** |
| `encode csv`                    | 156.10 | 112.40 | **1.4x** |
| `query: project 3 columns`      |  88.70 |  67.60 | **1.3x** |
| `encode pg-json`                |  67.80 |  53.90 |    1.26x |
| `encode ndjson`                 |  78.60 |  69.00 |    1.14x |

Zero cells regressed — the first screen in this audit with no movement to explain away. The
codec rows make sense: serialization reads every property of every element.

### Teeth: 11 tests, 3 of 3 mutants caught

| mutant                                            | result                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| replace the map entry instead of mutating the box | caught — 6 here, 28 in core |
| cache not cleared when the graph is reassigned    | caught                      |
| cache read without the detached guard             | caught                      |

Beyond the three invalidation cases: both element kinds, a write through either instance in
either order, the freeze still throwing, `setProperty`/`setProperties`/`removeProperty` round
trips, an element with no properties, and a property INDEX agreeing with a read made through a
second instance — the pairing the freeze exists to protect.

All seven byte-identity fuzzers are green on random seeds, which is the gate that matters most
for a change to the core data model: it touches what every codec and both engines read.

### A method note: `grep` cannot read `Graph.ts`

`grep` skips `packages/core/src/core/Graph.ts` as BINARY — `grep -n "Map<" Graph.ts` returns
nothing while `awk` and Python read the file fine, and `file` reports plain UTF-8. This is the
`rename-refactor-gotchas` note in the wild, and it cost a detour of believing the field was
declared somewhere else. **Use `awk`, Python or `rg` on that file**; a silent empty grep there is
not evidence of absence.

all seven byte-identity fuzzers green. No Rust changed.

## 162. The label read was the same hash lookup — 1.25-1.79x across the codecs and the GQL projection

Item 161 boxed the property read. The label read is the same shape in the same two files, and
this one came with its hypothesis already written down: the **rejected lever** in item 118
("reading `this.#id` instead of the `id` getter", measured flat) closed with

> What that getter costs is the string-keyed `Map.get` and the `Set` the caller iterates —
> neither of which the change touched.

That sentence named the real cost and left it alone. This item takes it.

### Pricing the read

Same fixture regime as item 161 so the two are comparable — 200,000 vertices with 1,000,000
edges RESIDENT, testing one label on each, min of seven:

|                                                         |       ms |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | -------: |
| `v.labels.has('P')` — what the engines do               |    18.84 |
| the getter with `.has` discarded                        |    12.71 |
| **a dense array of the same Sets — the CEILING**        | **2.20** |
| **a cached reference (an own property on the element)** | **2.79** |

94ns per label test, **67% of it the lookup** — the same split item 161 found for properties
(73%). And the second cost the old note named is real too: `[...v.labels]`, which is what every
codec does, ran 28.03ms against 7.42ms off a dense reference.

### A box, with two asymmetries the property path does not have

`Graph.elementLabels` now holds `{ set }`, and each element caches its box exactly as `#box`
caches the property box. Two things made this NOT a copy of item 161, and both were found by
pinning the current behaviour in a probe before writing any code:

- **A detached `Vertex` THROWS on `.labels`; a detached `Edge` reads `[]`.** `Vertex` writes
  `this.#graph!.elementLabels` and `Edge` writes `this.#graph?.`, so the two have never agreed —
  a raw `TypeError` on one, an empty set on the other. A cached box would have silently turned
  that throw into a successful read. It is preserved by keeping the cache EMPTY whenever the
  graph is: `evict()` and `set graph` both clear it, so a detached vertex still dereferences
  null and throws, with the identical message.
- **The returned `Set` is the graph's live, UNFROZEN object**, unlike the frozen property bag, so
  a caller may mutate it and a caller may hold it. The write paths build a fresh `Set` and
  REPLACE the old one, which means a held reference goes stale — so the box replaces `box.set`
  rather than mutating it in place. Mutating in place would have been a behaviour change
  disguised as an optimization.

Every write goes through one funnel, `Graph.commitElementLabels`, which mutates the box rather
than the map entry — the two-instances-share-an-id case from item 161, which is a real
construction path (`Graph.test.ts` itself does it).

### The write path, which this can only cost

A label write was one `Map.set`; through the funnel it is a `get` to find the box and then a
write. On an INSERT the `get` always misses, so ingest pays an extra hash probe per element.
That row went in its own process at min-of-seven, because the shared probe put it inside noise
AND leaning the wrong way — the case this audit has mis-read eight times.

| row                                  | before | box only | box + setter shortcut |
| ------------------------------------ | -----: | -------: | --------------------: |
| insert 200k vertices (1 label)       |  235.0 |    237.5 |                 238.2 |
| insert 200k vertices (2 labels)      |  241.3 |    241.4 |                 240.7 |
| **re-write labels on 200k vertices** |   29.9 | **32.0** |              **21.0** |
| `addLabel` on 200k vertices          |  202.4 |    192.3 |                 193.6 |
| CONTROL: insert, properties only     |  193.8 |    195.2 |                 193.7 |

The box alone made re-writing an element's labels **7% slower**, and that was a real cost, not
noise. The fix is that the setter already holds the box when it has read once, so it needs no
lookup at all — which turns that row into **1.42x FASTER than before** (29.9 → 21.0).

What remains is **+1% on insert** (235.0 → 238.2, against a dead-flat control at 193.8 → 193.7).
That is 16ns per element: exactly one failed hash probe, which is the honest and irreducible
price of finding a box to share. Recorded as the toll, not as noise.

### Measured, isolated, min-of-three, interleaved

| row                           |  before (min, range) |   after (min, range) |              ratio |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------: | -------------------: | -----------------: |
| `query: IS LABELED scan`      |    28.20 (28.2-29.2) |    15.75 (15.8-16.6) |          **1.79x** |
| `query: project 3 columns`    |    90.90 (90.9-97.1) |    53.58 (53.6-61.1) |          **1.70x** |
| `encode pg-json`              |    57.65 (57.7-72.3) |    39.61 (39.6-45.2) |          **1.46x** |
| `encode graphson`             | 178.29 (178.3-209.1) | 125.61 (125.6-164.7) |          **1.42x** |
| `encode csv`                  | 143.22 (143.2-154.2) | 114.78 (114.8-126.3) |          **1.25x** |
| CONTROL: `count(*)` over all  |                 0.04 |                 0.04 |               flat |
| CONTROL: property-only filter |    13.00 (13.0-13.8) |    11.65 (11.7-15.6) | flat (overlapping) |

Every moved row has NON-OVERLAPPING ranges and both controls are flat. The cross-engine screen
agrees on the `ts` column over two rounds a side (pg-json 52.5 → 32.9, graphson 166.9 → 108.7,
pg-text 88.8 → 72.7, csv 114.2 → 90.8, project 65.3 → 39.9) with the `ffi` column flat
throughout — the ideal control, since a TS core change cannot touch it. `encode ndjson`
(55.0 → 42.3) is left OUT of the claim: its ranges very nearly touch.

**The Gremlin bench shows nothing, and that is the right answer.** Every row is flat
(`V().out().has().count()` reads 119.9 before and 135.3 after, bracketing item 161's 128.1 from
both sides — a noisy row, not a signal). Those traversals read PROPERTIES, which item 161
already fixed, and their label steps are answered from label buckets. The probe predicted this
before the bench was run; the win for this item is in the GQL engine and the codecs.

### Teeth: 20 tests, 7 mutants, and one survivor that found a real gap

| mutant                                                  | result                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| replace the map entry instead of mutating the box       | caught — 13 failures   |
| funnel mutates the set in place instead of replacing    | caught — 1             |
| `evict()` keeps the label cache (detached vertex reads) | caught — 2             |
| `set graph` keeps the cache (reads the OLD graph)       | caught — 1             |
| `Edge.labels` loses its `?.` (detached edge throws)     | caught — 1             |
| the setter's shortcut assigns a FRESH box               | caught — 3             |
| **the setter's shortcut mutates in place**              | **SURVIVED 201 tests** |

The survivor is the point of doing this. The "held reference goes stale" case was tested through
`addLabelToVertex`, which goes through the graph's funnel — and the setter's shortcut is a
SEPARATE piece of code that nothing covered, so a behaviour change there was invisible. Two
tests later (a vertex and an edge) it dies. Each of the other six is killed by the one test
aimed at it, which is the mapping worth having: one pinned semantic, one guard.

**One test expectation of mine was wrong and the test said so.** I asserted that writing
`v.labels = ['Z']` would drop `v` from the `P` bucket of `verticesByLabel`. It does not: the raw
`labels` SETTER has never maintained the label index — only `addLabelToVertex` /
`removeLabelFromVertex` do. That is pre-existing, unrelated to the box, and now pinned as-is
with a note rather than quietly "fixed", because it is a different question from this item.

### Left on the table

- **One map instead of two.** `elementProperties` and `elementLabels` are now both
  `Map<id, box>` over the same key set. Merging them into one `Map<id, { bag, set }>` would make
  an element's first read find BOTH boxes in one lookup and would make insert _cheaper_ than
  before this item rather than 1% dearer. It churns item 161's just-shipped work and changes two
  public fields, so it is recorded here rather than bundled in.
- **Priming the cache on write.** The funnel could return the box so the setter populates
  `#lbox` on the FIRST write, making every element's first read free. Deliberately not done: the
  probes repeat, so rep 1 already warms the cache and none of them can measure it. Unmeasurable
  complexity is not an optimization.

## 163. Two headline bench rows used a predicate no vertex can satisfy — one ratio was 9.6x too big

Last item closed by naming the next target: merge `elementProperties` and `elementLabels` into one
`Map<id, { bag, set }>`. Priced against the alternatives it buys about **1% on insert** and one
lookup on an element's first read, while the screen still showed `traverse 1-hop + filter` at 65x
and `+ start filter` at 292x. So the map merge was deprioritized and those two rows were taken
instead — and neither turned out to be what it looked like.

### The fixture cannot satisfy the predicate

The bench builds every vertex with `age: i % 90`, so ages run 0..89. Both rows filter on
**`age > 500`**. Both return `count = 0`.

The row's own comment knew this and justified it:

> `age > 500` matches nothing (ages are 0..89), which does not reduce the work: the walk and the
> predicate still happen for every edge.

That is TRUE OF THE TS ENGINE and FALSE OF NATIVE, and the ratio is this table's entire output.
Measured across four selectivities on the same fixture:

| predicate                              | matches |     ts |   native |    ratio |
| -------------------------------------- | ------: | -----: | -------: | -------: |
| **far `> 500` (what the bench ran)**   |   **0** |   95.3 |     1.47 |  **65x** |
| far `> 85`                             |  44,440 |   94.4 |     1.51 |      63x |
| far `> 45`                             | 488,840 |   92.6 |     1.51 |      61x |
| far `>= 0`                             | 988,885 |  103.9 |     1.60 |      65x |
| **start `> 500` (what the bench ran)** |   **0** |   81.8 | **0.20** | **409x** |
| start `> 85`                           |  44,440 |   82.6 |     0.41 |     201x |
| start `> 45`                           | 488,840 |   73.7 |     2.39 |  **31x** |
| start `>= 0`                           | 988,885 | ~103.9 |     4.73 |     ~22x |

**The far row survives and the start row does not.** Native is flat at ~1.5ms on the far row
whether 0 or 988,885 edges match, because it scans the `age` column once either way — so that
65x is real, and the hypothesis that brought me here was wrong for it. The start row is a
different cost class by design (decide once per vertex, multiply by degree), which means native's
cost scales with how many starts MATCH: an empty predicate measured the cost of expanding
NOTHING. Its headline ratio spans **409x to 22x across thresholds alone**, and the empty end of
that range is what item 129 quoted as "the single widest gap in the cross-engine bench".

TS is flat across all of it (95.3 / 94.4 / 92.6 / 103.9), which is why the defect was invisible
from the TS side and why the row's comment was half right.

Both thresholds move to `> 45` — roughly half the edges, so both engines do real work and the two
rows stay comparable to each other. The corrected screen:

| row                             | was reported |       now |
| ------------------------------- | -----------: | --------: |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`       |          65x |     68.7x |
| `traverse 1-hop + start filter` |     **292x** | **30.6x** |

The quoted claim in `shortcuts.ts` is annotated rather than changed, because it is about the FAR
row and was re-verified under the correction. `bench-gremlin.ts` was checked and is already
correct (`gt(44)` against the same `i % 90` fixture, ~50% selectivity); the defect is confined to
these two rows.

### What the 68x actually consists of, priced for the next item

With the row now honest, the far gap is the largest remaining in the TS engine, so it was
profiled and priced rather than guessed at. The planner does reach the intended shape:
`farOnlyHopCount` is 89.2ms/rep inclusive, which is the whole query. Inside it:

|                                                                           | share of the query |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -----------------: |
| `farOnlyHopCount` itself (Map-of-Maps walk, degree sum, `binding.set`)    |              49.9% |
| the compiled property accessor `(env) => propOf(env.binding.get(v), key)` |          **38.3%** |
| the binary-op closure                                                     |               6.8% |
| `getVertexById`                                                           |               4.6% |
| **`get properties`**                                                      |           **0.2%** |

The property read is GONE as a cost — that is items 161 and 162 landing. What is left is the
expression layer: the walk puts the element INTO a Map and the compiled accessor takes it
straight back OUT, per evaluation, to read one property.

The walk evaluates once per VERTEX (200,000), not per edge, so each one costs ~446ns against
native's ~7ns. Priced layer by layer:

| layer, 200,000 vertices                                |    ms | delta |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ----: | ----: |
| `v.properties.age > 45`, element in hand — the CEILING |  1.73 |       |
| + `getVertexById(vid)`                                 |  5.66 | +3.93 |
| + `binding.set` then `binding.get`                     |  7.78 | +2.12 |
| + the compiled-closure shape                           |  8.05 | +0.27 |
| + `matchesLabel`                                       | 16.98 | +8.93 |

**The model totals 17ms and the real query is 89ms, and that discrepancy is the finding.** The
profile attributes 34.2ms/rep to the accessor this micro prices at ~2.4ms — a **14x gap**. That
is `harness-must-resemble-caller` exactly: in the engine that accessor is a MEGAMORPHIC call site
shared by every compiled expression shape, and a monomorphic micro cannot see it. So the target
for the next item is a direct evaluator for the common `<var>.<key> <cmp> <literal>` far
predicate, bypassing the binding round trip and the shared dispatch — with the warning attached
that the micro will understate the win, not overstate it.

Deliberately NOT concluded: that closures are expensive (+0.27ms says they are nearly free) or
that `getVertexById` is the problem (+3.93ms, real but a quarter of the accessor).

### The `@lenke/native:test` flake, finally characterized

Items 159-161 recorded this flake three times without capturing it. This time the full suite
exited 1, and chasing it produced the explanation: **nx prints its "Nx detected a flaky task"
banner from its own stored history, on PASSING runs too.** The run that exited 1 showed 38/39
tasks served from cache and that banner, with no failing test anywhere in the output.

Isolated and uncached, `@lenke/native:test` is 792 pass / 0 fail; five further uncached
FULL-SUITE runs all exit 0. So the banner is not a failure signal and should not be read as one —
which is most of why this looked like an intermittent failure across three items. The underlying
intermittent exit remains real but rare and still uncaptured; what is new is that the banner that
made it _look_ frequent is unrelated to whether the current run passed.

Gates separately: full TS suite exit 0 (after the above — one run exited 1, then five uncached
runs clean and the package isolated at 792 pass), `bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check`
exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green on random seeds. No engine code changed — this item
moves two bench thresholds and annotates a comment — so the bench screen IS the deliverable and
